analysis.one_liner: Bans making, selling, and using asbestos, with a two-year grace period for chlorine plants.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban commercial asbestos was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in March 2023 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Asbestos fibers cause fatal cancers, and the US still allows companies to import and use one type of asbestos. This bill would ban the manufacture, processing, use, and sale of commercial asbestos and products containing it, one year after passage. Two industries got carve-outs: chlorine plants could keep using asbestos diaphragms for two more years, and the President could grant national-security exemptions. The bill died in the Senate committee it was sent to, with no hearing or vote ever scheduled.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families — especially in plants, building trades, and auto repair, where asbestos fibers are released — would gain from an end to new asbestos entering commerce. Homeowners and the public would gain from EPA public-education materials on asbestos dangers and licensed removal services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and families exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it illegal, starting one year after enactment, for anyone to manufacture, process, use, or sell commercial asbestos or any product containing it.
Eight specific asbestos fiber types are covered, including chrysotile — the only type still imported into the United States, used mainly to make chlorine-production diaphragms.
It requires the EPA, with Health and Human Services, to create public education materials on asbestos health risks, federal prevention resources, and licensed asbestos removal services in each state.
Asbestos already installed in buildings before enactment is not covered, avoiding forced removal of existing materials.

analysis.who_pays: Chlorine producers (the chlor-alkali industry), which would have to replace asbestos diaphragms with alternatives within two years, and the small set of importers and manufacturers who sell asbestos or asbestos-containing products. Some transition costs could eventually show up in chemical prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chlorine producers and asbestos product makers

drawbacks.text: The ban is not immediate: chlor-alkali facilities in operation at enactment may keep importing, processing, and using asbestos fibers for chlorine production for two full years after enactment — the very use that accounts for nearly all remaining US asbestos imports.
Asbestos already installed in buildings stays in place; the bill regulates new commerce in asbestos, not removal of what is already there, so legacy exposure continues.

The President can grant national-security exemptions of up to three years, extendable once, so some uses could continue for up to six years with publication requirements and congressional notification.

Trace amounts of asbestos present as an 'impurity' in other chemicals are exempt, and the ban does not touch separate asbestos rules under cosmetics law, so coverage is narrower than a full toxic-substances ban.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case for banning asbestos is strong — asbestos fibers cause mesothelioma and other fatal cancers with no safe exposure level — and the bill gives the one major commercial user a two-year runway plus a national-security escape valve, which blunts the main transition-cost objection. The main design weakness is that it leaves legacy asbestos in buildings untouched and lets chlorine plants keep using it for two more years. Weighed honestly, this is a modest, carefully staged bill; its fate was decided by inaction, not by any vote on its merits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote, and Congress ended without any further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on March 30, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
Three senators, all Democrats, signed on as cosponsors.
That referral was the bill's last action: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion House action appears in its record before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The companies that import and use asbestos — chiefly chlor-alkali (chlorine) plants and asbestos product manufacturers — are better off because the ban never advanced; ordinary workers continue to face whatever exposure those ongoing uses create.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the asbestos ban and named it for Alan Reinstein, an asbestos-disease victim; the bill received no committee action after his introduction.

for.name: Three Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Added their names in support; no further action on the bill is recorded.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works (Chair Tom Carper)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the referral in March 2023 was the only committee action in its entire record.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and floor schedulers
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and there were no roll-call votes on the bill, so its support never grew beyond the Democratic side and its opposition was never recorded as a vote.

industries.note: Chlorine plants are the main remaining US user of asbestos, importing chrysotile for production diaphragms. The bill ends that use after a two-year grace period, so their interest in the bill's failure runs against removing a known carcinogen from commerce.

industries.industry: Asbestos importers and manufacturers of asbestos-containing products
industries.note: A ban on manufacture, processing, use, and sale after one year would shut off revenue from asbestos and products containing it. Their continued sales impose cancer-risk exposure on workers and consumers.

industries.industry: Asbestos abatement and licensed removal contractors
industries.note: The bill requires EPA to publicize licensed asbestos mitigation availability in every state, steering the public toward their services as awareness of exposure risks grows.
